A tool that visualises the merge of two git branches: what new features a merge brings in, and what might be lost by merging. Two things decide whether it succeeded:

+# VisualMerge
+
+**One-liner:** A drop-in web component that shows a developer who is not confident with git what a specific merge is about to do to their branch — what arrives, what changes, where git will stop.
+
+**Appetite:** A few weeks — 3 weeks / ~15 working days, one person · **Status:** draft · **Date:** 2026-08-16
+
+This is the first document in the repo. It was written before any code existed, by an unattended agent with no one to ask, so every judgement call is made here and marked. Assumptions are tagged `[ASSUMPTION]` with what would change if they are wrong.
+
+---
+
+## Problem
+
+Git merges are decided by people who cannot predict them.
+
+The concrete moment: someone has a branch, `main` has moved since they branched, and they are about to press a button — merge `main` into their branch, or merge their PR. They want to know three things and can find out none of them:
+
+1. Will this stop and ask me something?
+2. Does anything of *mine* get changed by this?
+3. What does the file actually look like afterwards?
+
+**GitHub cannot answer 2 or 3, structurally.** A PR's "Files changed" is a three-dot diff — `git diff $(git merge-base main head) head` — so the left-hand side is frozen at the moment the branch diverged. Everything that landed on `main` since then is *outside the diff entirely*. I reproduced this: `main` adds an `audit()` call to `refund()`, `feature` adds a `log()` call to `charge()`, both in `pay.py`. The PR diff shows one inserted line. The merged file — which neither author has ever seen and neither will review — has both. Git merged it cleanly and silently, and the PR page is not lying so much as answering a different question. GitHub's own docs claim on the same page that Files changed "shows what would change if the pull request merged," which is a two-dot claim pasted onto a three-dot view. The complaint thread ([community #14528](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/14528), open since April 2022, 74 👍, no staff response) includes a production incident caused by exactly this.
+
+For question 1, GitHub gives a banner with a list of conflicting *file names* and no content. Seeing the conflict requires clicking into the web editor, which carries the warning that resolving there "merges the entire base branch into the head branch" — the only native way to see the conflict is to mutate your branch.
+
+**The audience I am building for is the junior developer on a team** — under two years in, bootcamp grad or first job, comfortable with `commit` and `push`, not comfortable with `merge`. Chosen over the alternatives deliberately:
+
+- **The designer reviewing a PR** does not press the merge button and does not have a repo. They need a rendered preview, not a merge explanation. Different product.
+- **The student** is already served. learnGitBranching (33.9k stars, commits as of 2026-08-11) owns git education, is free, and is better at it than a three-week project will be. It simulates git; it has no real repo. That is the right design for teaching and the wrong one here.
+- **The open-source drive-by contributor** has the problem and the lowest possible willingness to install anything or read a docs page. They are a beneficiary if the maintainer embeds the widget, not the person to design for.
+
+The junior on a team is the only audience with all four of: real stakes, a real repo, the problem recurring weekly, and *someone nearby with the motivation to install a tool for them*. That last point is the whole reason this is embeddable rather than a CLI: **the person who installs VisualMerge is not the person who reads it.** The installer is a team lead, docs maintainer, or internal-tooling developer. The reader is the junior. Both have to be served, and they want opposite things — the installer wants two lines and no infrastructure, the reader wants plain English.
+
+What they do today instead: press the button and find out; or ask a senior, who spends five minutes on it; or avoid merging until the branch is so far behind that the merge is genuinely hard. The cost is a mix of interrupted seniors, a class of bug that gets attributed to "a bad merge" and never diagnosed, and juniors learning by trauma.
+
+## Why now / why at all
+
+**The honest case against, first.** Every attempt to sell this has failed. MergeBetter shut down on 2026-02-11. SemanticMerge was absorbed into Unity and its site 404s. Crystal (Brun et al., FSE 2011 Distinguished Paper) did speculative background merging and its implementation has 7 stars and last commit 2015. The GitHub topic `merge-preview` contains one repository, 2 stars, dead since 2020. Every Show HN in this space scored in single digits, while merge *resolution* tools and VCS replacements got front pages. The pattern is consistent enough to be a finding: **people will pay for a tool that does the merge better; they do not seek out a tool that explains it.** They do not believe they have this problem until after they have lost work.
+
+The counter-argument is the reason to build anyway: the failed attempts were all products — desktop apps, paid services, background daemons, accounts. This is a component, and the cost of adoption is a script tag on a page someone already maintains. It does not need anyone to believe they have a problem before they encounter it; it needs one team lead to put it where the problem happens. That is a much lower bar, and it has not been tried.
+
+There is a genuine reason it is buildable now that it was not in 2011: **`git merge-tree --write-tree`** (git 2.38, October 2022) computes a full `ort` merge — content merge, rename detection, directory/file conflicts, recursive ancestors — without a working tree and without touching the index. Crystal had to keep a fleet of clones and run real merges in them. This is one subprocess call. Verified locally on git 2.39.5: conflicted merge exits 1 and emits the result tree OID, index stages 1/2/3 per conflicted path, and NUL-delimited typed conflict records; clean merge exits 0 with just a tree OID; both work in a bare repo. GitLab's Gitaly adopted it. No reader-facing tool has.
+
+**Buy-versus-build:** nothing to buy. No maintained web component renders a merge. `@gitgraph/js` was archived 2024-07-13. `@codemirror/merge` is two-way only (a regression from CodeMirror 5, which is itself archived). Monaco's three-way merge editor is VS Code workbench code, not in the OSS package, and was closed "not planned" twice. GitHub's API will tell you *that* a PR conflicts and never *where*. The rendering primitives (`diff2html` at 12.6 KB gzip, `node-diff3`) exist and are maintained; the thing that combines them does not.
+
+If this is never built: nothing much happens. Juniors keep learning by trauma. That is the honest answer, and it is why the appetite is three weeks and not a quarter.
+
+## Goals
+
+1. A person who does not understand git can look at a specific real merge and correctly say what it will do — conflicts, arrivals, and changes to their own work.
+2. Putting it on a web page costs two lines and no infrastructure.
+3. It is never wrong. A confident wrong answer is worse than no tool, because the audience has no way to detect it.
+
+## Non-goals
+
+The brief is right that these matter more than the goals. Anything left ambiguous here, a later run will build.
+
+| Not this | Why |
+|---|---|
+| **A merge conflict *resolver*** | Read-only, always. No edit, no "accept theirs", no write to the repo. Resolving needs write access, auth, and undo; it doubles the scope and GitHub/Copilot are pouring money into that direction. |
+| **A git client** | No clone, fetch, checkout, commit, push, rebase. Not even a button that runs the merge. |
+| **A code review tool** | No comments, threads, approvals, or review state. |
+| **A CI integration** | No GitHub App, no Action, no bot posting PR comments in v1. The CLI can be *run by* CI — that is the host's business, not ours. |
+| **A general diff viewer** | It shows the merge-relevant slice with capped context. No file tree, no syntax highlighting (that alone costs more than the entire size budget), no whole-file browsing. |
+| **A commit graph renderer** | This is the single most tempting rabbit hole. No DAG layout algorithm, no lane assignment, no curves. A junior does not read a DAG, and there is no evidence that a prettier graph answers any of the six questions below. |
+| **A git teaching tool** | learnGitBranching exists, is maintained and is better. VisualMerge explains *one specific real merge*, not the concept of merging. |
+| **A hosted service** | No accounts, no backend we run, no data leaving the host's control. |
+| **Semantic / AST-aware merging** | Text and paths only. Mergiraf does tree-sitter merging; that is a separate universe. |
+| **Octopus merges, submodules, rebase preview, cherry-pick preview, multi-repo** | Two-parent merges only. Everything else degrades honestly (see below), it does not get supported. |
+| **A merge queue** | Mergify, Kodiak, Aviator and GitHub Merge Queue exist and solve a different problem for a different buyer. |
+
+## What "an inexperienced programmer can tell what the merge is doing" means
+
+Turned into something checkable. **Six questions.** A viewer must answer these correctly from the visualisation alone, with no git knowledge and no access to the repo:
+
+| # | Question | Why it is on the list |
+|---|---|---|
+| Q1 | If I do this merge, will git stop and ask me something? (yes/no) | The single most-asked question. Binary, unambiguous, gradeable. |
+| Q2 | Which files will it stop on? | GitHub answers this one. It is the floor, not the target. |
+| Q3 | Name one thing that arrives on my branch that was not there before. | "What does the merge bring in" — the operator's first requirement. |
+| Q4 | Does any line of my own work get changed or removed by this merge? Which file? | The question nothing on the market answers. |
+| Q5 | For file `X`: afterwards, does it have my change, their change, both, or neither? | The `pay.py` case. Tests whether the person understands the *result*, not just the inputs. |
+| Q6 | Is there anything here you would not merge without asking someone first? | Tests calibration, not recall. A viewer who says "yes" to a clean 3-file merge is being alarmed, not informed. |
+
+### Defining "lost", precisely
+
+The brief says "what might be lost by merging", and it would be easy to overclaim here and build a tool that cries wolf. A default three-way merge does **not** silently drop committed work in the general case. What it actually does, and what the tool may honestly report as loss, is exactly four things:
+
+- **L1 — Conflict.** Git stops. Someone will pick a side, and whichever side loses is lost. The tool shows both sides so the person picking knows what they are discarding.
+- **L2 — Modify/delete, rename/rename, rename/delete.** One side changed a file the other side removed or moved. Verified: git reports these as distinct typed conflicts.
+- **L3 — Your file's content changes.** `git diff <your-branch> <merge-result>` — files on your branch whose content is different after the merge. Mostly additions, but this is the honest answer to Q4 and it is computable exactly.
+- **L4 — Silent combination.** A clean merge producing a file neither author wrote nor reviewed. Not "loss" but the same failure mode: the `pay.py` demo. Flagged, never alarmed.
+
+If it is not one of those four, the tool says nothing. Overclaiming loss is the fastest route to being ignored.
+
+### How the claim gets tested, with no research budget
+
+**Instrument:** five fixture repos with known correct answers, six questions each, one Google Form, unmoderated, ~10 minutes. Fixtures: (a) trivially clean, nothing interesting; (b) the `pay.py` silent combination; (c) a content conflict in one file; (d) modify/delete plus a rename; (e) a messy one — 40 files, three conflicts, one rename/rename.
+
+**Participants:** eight people who self-report "not confident with git", recruited from wherever they can be found — a bootcamp cohort, colleagues' juniors, a Discord. **This is a smoke test, not research.** n=8 detects "this is incomprehensible"; it does not measure anything to two significant figures, and the document should not pretend otherwise.
+
+**Baseline:** the same six questions against **GitHub's PR page for the identical merge**, which is free to construct and is the actual status quo. `[ASSUMPTION]` the baseline is **2/6** — Q1 and Q2 partly answerable from the conflict banner, Q3 partly from the commit list, Q4 and Q5 not answerable at all because of the three-dot diff, Q6 a coin flip. **If the measured baseline comes in at 4/6 or better, the premise of this project is weaker than I think and the appetite should be cut to a weekend spike.** Measuring it is milestone 0 and it costs half a day.
+
+**Target:** **≥5 of 6 correct for ≥6 of 8 participants**, with two hard sub-targets — **Q1 correct 8/8** (a tool that gets "will it conflict" wrong for anyone is broken) and **Q4 correct ≥6/8** (it is the differentiated claim). Cap: 90 seconds per merge; slower than that and it is not usable in the moment it is needed.
+
+**Continuous cheap version:** one person, read-aloud, recorded, at every milestone including the first. This is the binding gate — not the survey.
+
+## What "easily integrateable into websites" means
+
+**The acceptance criterion, stated as code.** A host page adds exactly this and nothing else:
+
+```html
+<script type="module" src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/visual-merge@1.0.0/dist/visual-merge.js?register"></script>
+<visual-merge src="/merges/pr-482.json"></visual-merge>
+```
+
+**The host supplies:** one JSON file at a URL. That is the entire contract.
+
+**It must NOT require:** a bundler, a framework, npm, a `package.json`, a build step on the host, an API key or OAuth flow, a CORS proxy, cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP), a git binary or WASM git in the browser, the repo to be public, a server that we run, or a change to the host's Content-Security-Policy.
+
+That last one has a design consequence, so it is decided here rather than discovered later: **all styling goes through `adoptedStyleSheets`, never a `<style>` element in the shadow root.** A `<style>` in a shadow root is subject to the host's `style-src`; constructed stylesheets are not covered by CSP at all (deliberately — WICG/construct-stylesheets#98). That single choice makes the widget work under `style-src 'self'` with zero host cooperation. Related decided defaults: autonomous custom element (Baseline Widely available since 2020), shadow DOM with `:host { all: initial; display: block }` and its own box-sizing reset, `px`/`em` and never `rem` (`:root` does not match inside a shadow tree, so a host doing `html { font-size: 62.5% }` would shred the layout), namespaced `--vm-*` custom properties plus `::part()` for theming, and a `?register` query-param opt-in for custom-element registration so two copies on one page cannot crash with `NotSupportedError`.
+
+**Size budget: 30 KB gzip target, 50 KB hard ceiling, no eager dependency over 15 KB.** Derived from the 300 KB compressed-JS critical-path budget for a P75 mobile device — an optional widget cannot defensibly claim more than 10% of a page's entire JS allowance. This disqualifies, as eager dependencies: d3-full (90 KB), Chart.js (48 KB), ECharts even in a custom build (172 KB), Monaco (580 KB), Mermaid (949 KB UMD). Hand-built SVG/DOM, `diff2html`'s parser (12.6 KB), or a hand-picked d3 subset are what fit. Anything heavier goes behind a lazy `import()`.
+
+**Time-to-first-render: ≤10 minutes** from opening the README to seeing your own merge on your own page, on a machine with nothing installed. Measured by doing it, not estimated.
+
+### The hard constraint: a browser cannot run git — decided, not deferred
+
+Somebody has to compute the merge. Four candidates, and this is **decided**, because deferring it would leave the most consequential choice in the project to whoever reads this next.
+
+| Option | Verdict |
+|---|---|
+| **isomorphic-git in-browser** (v1.41.4, 68 KB gzip, actively released) | **Rejected.** It throws `MergeNotSupportedError` when there are multiple merge bases — `// TODO: Recursive Merge strategy` is in the source — and has no rename detection anywhere. It fails on precisely the merges worth visualising, and it needs the whole repo in IndexedDB plus a CORS proxy to get it there. |
+| **wasm-git** (libgit2 1.9.4) | **Rejected for v1.** Real merge semantics, but 360–545 KB of compressed wasm against a 30 KB budget. Ten times over on its own. |
+| **GitHub API** | **Rejected as a data source.** REST `compare` has no conflict field at all; `mergeable` is a tri-state that requires a PR to exist and polling while it computes. It can tell you *that* it conflicts, never *where*. Plus 60 requests/hour unauthenticated, which puts a token in the browser — banned. |
+| **A CLI producing a JSON file** | **Chosen.** |
+
+**Decision: the merge is computed outside the browser by a small Node CLI that shells out to `git merge-tree --write-tree -z` and emits one JSON file. The widget renders that JSON and nothing else.**
+
+Verified locally (git 2.39.5): works in a bare repo, does not read or write the working tree or index, sub-second, exit 0 clean / exit 1 conflicts, full typed conflict records. The JSON is a static asset — it can be produced in CI, in a docs build, in a pre-commit hook, or by hand. **No server is required for v1.** A server is the same CLI behind an HTTP handler and is deliberately a later, optional milestone.
+
+Three consequences to accept now: the JSON contains source code, so the host must not publish it accidentally (the README says this in bold, and a `--no-content` mode emits paths and verdicts only); the widget is testable entirely from fixtures with no git anywhere near the test suite; and the "paste two branch names, get a merge" experience does not exist in v1.
+
+**Falsification condition:** if the dominant demand turns out to be "point it at a GitHub PR URL with zero setup", this decision is wrong and the right answer is a small hosted service. That is a different product with auth, hosting cost and a privacy story, and it is out of appetite. It is not a pivot to make quietly.
+
+## Success criteria
+
+| Metric | Baseline today | Target | How measured | Checked when |
+|---|---|---|---|---|
+| Comprehension: median correct of 6 questions | `[ASSUMPTION]` 2/6 on GitHub's PR page — **measured in M0** | ≥5/6 for ≥6 of 8 participants | Form, 5 fixtures, 8 self-reported non-confident git users | M4 |
+| Q1 "will it conflict" correct | unknown; GitHub gives a banner, no data | 8/8 | Same instrument | M4 |
+| Q4 "does my work get touched" correct | 0/8 — GitHub cannot answer it | ≥6/8 | Same instrument | M4 |
+| Time to answer all six | n/a | ≤90 s median per merge | Timed in the form | M4 |
+| **Correctness: widget verdict vs real `git merge`** | n/a | **100% agreement, 25+ fixtures** | Harness runs a real merge in a throwaway clone, asserts conflict set and result tree OID match the JSON | M2, then every commit |
+| Host integration | n/a | **≤2 lines**, 0 build steps, 0 tokens | The README snippet is the test; a plain `.html` file in `examples/` must work by double-clicking it | M4 |
+| Time-to-first-render for a new host | n/a | ≤10 min | Timed run-through on a clean machine | M4 |
+| **Guardrail — bundle size** | n/a | ≤30 KB gzip, **hard fail >50 KB** | CI check on `dist/`, fails the build | Every commit from M1 |
+| **Guardrail — no false calm** | n/a | **Zero** cases where the widget says "clean" and git conflicts | Differential harness; any occurrence is P0 | Every commit |
+| **Guardrail — no host CSP change** | n/a | Renders correctly under `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'` | A fixture page served with that header in CI | M4 |
+
+## Solution sketch
+
+Three pieces, one of which is deliberately dumb.
+
+**1. `visual-merge` CLI (Node, no deps beyond what's needed).**
+`npx visual-merge main feature -o merge.json`. Verifies `git --version >= 2.38` at startup and fails with an explicit message otherwise. Then:
+
+- `git merge-tree --write-tree -z <ours> <theirs>` → result tree OID, conflicted index stages, typed conflict records.
+- `git diff -M --name-status <ours> <resultTree>` → **the answer to Q4**: what happens to *your* branch.
+- `git diff -M --name-status <theirs> <resultTree>` → what happens to theirs.
+- `git log <ours>..<theirs>` and the reverse → commits arriving in each direction.
+- `git cat-file` for the hunks that get rendered, capped.
+
+Emits versioned JSON: `{schemaVersion, ours, theirs, mergeBase, willConflict, files: [{path, verdict, loss, hunks}], arriving: {commits, files}, unsupported: []}`.
+
+Two parsing traps, both hit and confirmed during research, that will silently produce "zero conflicts" if missed: the `-z` messages section **starts with its own NUL**, so there is a double-NUL after the last stage entry and a naive parser reads it as end-of-stream; and each conflict message has a trailing `\n` *inside* its NUL-delimited field. Also: only the `CONFLICT (…)` short type is stable (git's own source says "relied upon by external tools… DO NOT change any of these strings"); the human-readable message is not, so nothing may parse it. Both-modified and add/add both collapse to `CONFLICT (contents)` — distinguish them from stage presence (2+3 without 1 = add/add) rather than from the message text.
+
+**2. The widget** — `<visual-merge src="...">`, a custom element with a shadow root. Three levels, in comprehension order rather than data order:
+
+- **The verdict.** One sentence, large: *"Git will stop and ask you about 2 files."* or *"This merges cleanly. 3 of your files change."* This alone answers Q1 and is most of what most viewers need.
+- **The file list.** One row per affected file, each with a plain-English verdict — "you get their version", "both changes combine, cleanly", "git will stop here", "this file was moved on both sides". Loss category L1–L4 shown as a plain phrase, never a git term.
+- **The file detail**, on click. Yours, theirs, and the result. Conflict regions rendered as two labelled panes, never as `<<<<<<<` markers, which are exactly the thing the audience cannot read.
+
+No graph. If the topology needs saying, it is a sentence: *"Their branch has 4 commits you don't have. Yours has 2 they don't."*
+
+**3. The honest-degradation path.** The CLI whitelists what it understands: two-parent merges, text files, renames. Everything else — submodules, binary conflicts, octopus, distinct modes, directory-rename collisions — lands in `unsupported[]` and the widget renders *"There is something here I can't explain: <git's own message>. Ask someone before merging."* Refusing to answer is a feature. It is what keeps the "never wrong" goal achievable inside three weeks.
+
+## Alternatives considered
+
+- **Do nothing.** Defensible. See "Why now" — the demand signal in this space is genuinely bad. The reason to proceed is that the cost of the experiment is three weeks and the distribution mechanism (a script tag) has not been tried.
+- **Buy / reuse.** Nothing to buy — surveyed desktop clients, web libraries, educational tools, diff components, GitHub/GitLab natively, and 25 years of academic work. GitKraken's "Conflict Prevention" and Tower's branch comparison flag overlapping *file paths*; GitLens does a real dry run for `pull` only and returns an integer. None show the merge result. Reviewable is the only product that has written the problem down (it has a gutter marker for base-branch-only lines) and it is a better diff base, not a merge preview.
+- **Reuse a renderer instead of building one.** Partly adopted: `diff2html`'s parser (12.6 KB, maintained) is a candidate for hunk parsing. Rejected as a *renderer* because it flattens combined diffs to two columns and because a general diff view is an explicit non-goal.
+- **A VS Code extension instead of a web component.** Rejected: it fails goal 2 outright, and the moment of failure — pressing merge on a PR page — is usually in a browser.
+- **A hosted service with a GitHub App.** Rejected: auth, hosting, privacy, and a permission grant on the user's repos, all outside a three-week appetite. This is the shape every dead predecessor took.
+
+## Constraints and assumptions
+
+**Hard constraints**
+- Browsers cannot run git. Merge computation happens elsewhere. (Addressed above.)
+- `git merge-tree --write-tree` needs **git ≥ 2.38**. Ubuntu 22.04 LTS ships 2.34.1 and is in standard support until May 2027 — the one real gap. Debian 12/13, Ubuntu 24.04+, RHEL 8+, macOS 15+ and all GitHub Actions runners are fine.
+- `merge-tree` writes dangling objects into the ODB. A long-lived server repo needs periodic `git gc --prune`. The ODB must be writable.
+- Read-only against the host's repo. Never write, never mutate, never run `git merge`.
+
+**Assumptions** — each with what changes if it is wrong
+- `[ASSUMPTION]` The GitHub baseline is ~2/6. → If it is 4+/6, the problem is smaller than stated; cut to a weekend spike. Measured in M0.
+- `[ASSUMPTION]` Eight recruitable non-confident git users exist within reach. → If not, fall back to n=3 read-alouds and drop the survey; the number becomes directional, and the doc must say so rather than quoting it as a metric.
+- `[ASSUMPTION]` A capped JSON for a typical PR is well under 1 MB. → If real merges routinely blow that, content moves behind a lazy per-file fetch and the "one static file" contract weakens to "one file plus a directory".
+- `[ASSUMPTION]` A team lead willing to embed this exists. This is the whole distribution theory and it is untested. → If no one will embed it, the artefact is still a CLI plus a local HTML page, which is a smaller and less interesting product.
+- `[ASSUMPTION]` Plain-English per-file verdicts are more comprehensible than a graph. That is the central design bet, and M1 exists to test it before three weeks are spent on it.
+
+## Milestones
+
+**M0 — Measure the baseline** (½ day, part of week 1). Build the five fixture repos. Push each to a scratch GitHub repo, open the PR, screenshot what a reader actually sees, answer the six questions from it, write the number down. Without this there is no baseline and the success criteria are unfalsifiable.
+
+**M1 — Walking skeleton** (~4 days). CLI → JSON → static page → real human. `node bin/visual-merge.js main feature -o merge.json`, one hand-written HTML file with a `<script type="module">` and `<visual-merge src>`, rendering the verdict sentence and the file list for one real merge in one real repo. Ugly. Hardcoded colours. No graph, no file detail, no CDN, no npm. Ends with **one inexperienced person reading it aloud and answering the six questions**. That gate is binding — see kill criteria.
+
+**M2 — The file-level story, and correctness** (~4 days). Per-file plain-English verdicts across all four loss categories. `unsupported[]` and the honest-degradation panel. **The differential harness**: for every fixture, run a real `git merge` in a throwaway clone and assert the JSON's conflict set and result tree OID match. 25+ fixtures including rename/rename, modify/delete, add/add, criss-cross history, binary, submodule, deleted directory. Independently valuable: at this point the CLI is a usable thing on its own.
+
+**M3 — The line-level story** (~3 days). Click a file, see yours / theirs / result. Conflict regions as two labelled panes. Context capped. No syntax highlighting. Independently valuable: this is the first version that answers Q5 well.
+
+**M4 — Packaging and the comprehension test** (~3 days). Single ESM bundle, shadow DOM with `adoptedStyleSheets`, `?register` guard, `::part()` theming, `<title>`/`<desc>`/data-table **inside the shadow root** (ARIA IDREFs do not cross a shadow boundary, so keeping the whole relationship in one tree is the only approach that works everywhere today), size check in CI, CSP fixture page, self-host tarball, README with the two-line snippet. Then **run the eight-person comprehension test and write the number down, whatever it says.**
+
+~15 days. The project is killable after each milestone with something usable left behind.
+
+## Definition of done — M1
+
+- [ ] `node bin/visual-merge.js <ours> <theirs> -o merge.json` runs in any git repo and exits non-zero with a readable message if git < 2.38.
+- [ ] The JSON has a `schemaVersion` and validates against a checked-in schema.
+- [ ] The parser handles the `-z` double-NUL section separator and the trailing newline inside message fields, with a unit test for each that fails against the naive implementation.
+- [ ] Conflict classification reads only git's stable `CONFLICT (…)` short types and index stage presence — never the human-readable message. Enforced by a test.
+- [ ] `examples/basic.html` renders the verdict sentence and file list from a JSON file, opened by double-clicking, with no server and no build.
+- [ ] The widget renders `merge-clean.json` and `merge-conflicted.json` fixtures identically in Chrome, Firefox and Safari.
+- [ ] Tests: fixture repos built by a script, not committed as binaries; `npm test` green from a clean clone.
+- [ ] The CI size check exists and passes, even though the bundle is tiny at this point.
+- [ ] **One person who self-reports as not confident with git has read one real merge aloud and answered the six questions, and their answers — including the wrong ones — are written into `docs/01-comprehension-log.md`.**
+- [ ] `docs/00-shape.md` updated wherever M0's measured baseline contradicts it.
+
+## Risks and rabbit holes
+
+| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| **Nobody wants it** — every predecessor died | High | Fatal | Cannot be mitigated, only tested cheaply. Three-week appetite; M1's read-aloud is the earliest signal. Named in paragraph one, not buried here. |
+| **Rendering a commit graph.** The most attractive way to burn a week | High | High | Banned by non-goal. Hard rule: **no automatic layout algorithm in v1.** Topology is a sentence. |
+| **Supporting every git edge case.** Octopus, submodules, binary, distinct modes, directory-rename collisions | High | High | Whitelist + `unsupported[]` + an honest "I can't explain this one" panel. Refusing is cheaper and safer than a wrong answer. |
+| **Building a general diff viewer.** Syntax highlighting alone exceeds the entire size budget | Medium | High | Non-goal; the CI size check makes it fail the build rather than fail a review. |
+| **GitHub API auth.** Tokens, OAuth, rate limits | Medium | High | The API is not a data source. Banned outright. If a fixture needs a real PR, fetch it offline with the user's own credentials. |
+| **A wrong answer.** Says "clean", git conflicts | Medium | Fatal to trust | The differential harness in M2 is the whole answer. Any occurrence is P0. This is the reason M2 is not deferred. |
+| **Overclaiming loss** and becoming a tool that cries wolf | Medium | Medium | Loss is defined as exactly L1–L4. Nothing else is reported as loss. |
+| **Plain English is harder than it looks.** Writing a per-file verdict that is short, true, and not condescending | High | Medium | This is the actual product work. Budget it as such: M1's read-aloud is about the wording, not the code. |
+| **Ubuntu 22.04's git 2.34.1** | Low | Low | Explicit version check with a clear message. Fallback is a throwaway worktree + `git merge --no-commit`; **timeboxed to 1 day** and only if a real user hits it. |
+| **JSON contains source code, host publishes it by accident** | Medium | High for that host | Bold warning in the README; `--no-content` mode; the example writes to a path that is gitignored by default. |
+| **Duplicate `customElements.define()`** crashing a host page that also bundles the widget | Low | Medium | `?register` opt-in pattern, plus a guard. |
+
+## Non-functional requirements
+
+- **Size:** ≤30 KB gzip, hard fail above 50 KB, enforced in CI from M1.
+- **Security:** no tokens anywhere, in code, tests or examples. No network calls from the widget except fetching its own `src`. Nothing is `eval`'d. The CLI never writes to the repo it inspects and never runs `git merge`.
+- **Privacy:** the JSON contains source code and stays under the host's control. No telemetry, ever — not analytics, not error reporting.
+- **Accessibility:** SVG with `role="img"` and `aria-labelledby` → `<title>`/`<desc>`; a "view as table" toggle as the long description (a data table is the WAI-sanctioned long alternative — and note `aria-describedby` flattens its target to a string, so it must never point at the table). All ARIA relationships stay inside the shadow root. The verdict sentence must be readable by a screen reader without touching the visualisation.
+- **Errors:** malformed JSON, a schema version mismatch, or a fetch failure render a visible message in the widget. Never a blank box, never a silent console error — a blank box reads as "no problems found" to this audience.
+- **Licensing:** MIT. Check every dependency; `mergely` is GPL/commercial dual and CodeMirror 5 is archived.
+- **Browsers:** last two versions of Chrome, Firefox, Safari. No IE, no polyfills, no transpilation below ES2022.
+
+## Kill criteria
+
+Decided now, while nobody is attached to it.
+
+1. **M0 says the baseline is 4+/6.** GitHub already answers the questions well enough; cut to a weekend spike or stop.
+2. **M1's read-aloud: the person cannot answer Q1 correctly.** Stop coding and redesign the presentation. If a second redesign also fails, the design bet — plain-English verdicts over a graph — is wrong, and that is worth knowing after five days rather than fifteen.
+3. **M4 comprehension lands below baseline + 2 questions.** The tool does not work. Publish the finding, do not ship the tool.
+4. **The differential harness disagrees with real git on any fixture and it cannot be fixed in a day.** Stop. A tool this audience cannot check is worse than no tool.
+5. **After M2, the honest verdict on >90% of real merges is "nothing interesting happens."** The problem is rarer than assumed; ship the CLI as a small utility and stop.
+
+## Decisions I need
+
+Answerable with "defaults are fine."
+
+1. **Data source: CLI-produced JSON, no server, no in-browser git.** *(Default: yes — decided above. Flag it now if the real ask was "paste a GitHub PR URL and it just works", because that is a hosted service and a different project.)*
+2. **Primary audience: the junior developer on a team, with the team lead as installer.** *(Default: yes. If the actual intended reader is a student, stop — learnGitBranching already wins that.)*
+3. **No commit graph, ever, in v1.** *(Default: yes. This is the biggest single scope saving in the document.)*
+4. **Appetite is three weeks and M4 ships whatever comprehension number it measures, including a bad one.** *(Default: yes.)*
+5. **npm package name `visual-merge`, element `<visual-merge>`, MIT.** *(Default: yes — check npm availability in M4, not now.)*

+### Top open question for the implementation-plan run
+
+Not the compute location — that is decided. It is **which JSON-production path the README leads with**, because it determines what the first ten minutes of a new host's experience feels like:
+
+- **(a) "Run our CLI in your repo, commit the JSON, point the widget at it."** Zero infrastructure, works today, but the JSON goes stale the moment either branch moves.
+- **(b) "Run the CLI in CI on every PR and publish the JSON as an artefact."** Always fresh, but now the host needs a workflow file and somewhere to serve artefacts.
+- **(c) "Run `visual-merge serve` and point the widget at `localhost`."** Always fresh and zero staleness, but it is a server, which v1 said it would not need.
+
+My recommendation is **(a) as the documented path with the staleness caveat printed in the widget itself** — the JSON carries the two commit OIDs it was computed from, and the widget shows "computed from commits abc123 / def456" so a stale render is visibly stale rather than quietly wrong. (b) and (c) become recipes in the README, not product surface. But this deserves ten minutes of thought at the start of the implementation plan rather than being inherited silently from this sentence.
